title: Order events
subDomain: who finds out when an order ships

act2.summary: a fraud hold must silence the customer-facing notifications (email, sms) while the internal bookkeeping (inventory, analytics) keeps firing exactly as before

solutions.title: Four independent observers, subscribed to one subject
solutions.tradeoff: Each consumer becomes its own class, none aware the others exist - exactly the decoupling act 1 rewards. But act 2's rule isn't about any one observer, it's about splitting the whole set into two groups that get notified differently, and a flat list of equal subscribers has no way to say that: the subject itself had to grow a second list and a second subscribe method before the hold could be expressed at all.

solutions.title: One class, one method, that already sequences the whole fan-out
solutions.tradeoff: dispatch() was already the one place that named the order consumers run in - wrapping the last two calls in a condition is a two-line change inside a method that already existed for exactly this reason. The price was paid in act 1: the mediator has to know all four consumers by name, which is the coupling Observer's independent classes exist to avoid.

solutions.title: A chain of links, any one of which can stop the rest
solutions.tradeoff: Stopping the chain is this pattern's whole idea, so a fraud link that returns false to silence what follows reads as exactly what it is. It just isn't quite the cheapest way to get there: the new link is a fifth array entry plus its own file update, one file and one hunk more than the route that only had to touch a single existing method.

reviewFocus: Does the chosen candidate's WALKTHROUGH.md name what would change my mind about the choice, or does it just describe the code?

In the observer route, was splitting one subscriber list into subscribeAlways/subscribeConditional actually the cheapest way to express 'these two groups differ', or could a single list with a per-observer flag have done it for less?

In the chain-of-responsibility route, does inserting fraudLink between analyticsLink and emailLink actually preserve act 1's order for a clean order - and would inserting it anywhere else have broken that?

Is 'dispatch() already named the one sequence, so guarding two lines of it is the cheapest possible change' a fair reading of why mediator wins here - and would a reader's CHOICE.md, written before act 2, have said the same thing?
Do all three routes - and the no-pattern baseline - agree, byte for byte, on which four consumers fire, in what order, for a clean order?
